sections.text: Classical Greek rhetoric developed in the 5th century BCE in Athens and Sicily as a response to democratic institutions that required citizens to speak in courts, assemblies, and public occasions. Aristotle systematized it in the 4th century; it became the dominant intellectual discipline of the Hellenistic and Roman world.

```
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|            CLASSICAL GREEK RHETORIC — LANDSCAPE                  |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                  |
|  HISTORICAL CONTEXT                                              |
|  Athenian democracy: citizens must argue their own cases        |
|  Sicily (5th c. BCE): Corax and Tisias — first rhetorical       |
|  handbooks after the tyrants fell and property suits arose      |
|                                                                  |
|  THE SOPHISTS (5th c. BCE)                                       |
|  Protagoras: man is the measure of all things                   |
|  Gorgias: logos can produce any effect; praise of Helen         |
|  Thrasymachus: justice is what benefits the stronger            |
|  Teaching "virtue" (arete) for fees; rhetoric as power tool    |
|                                                                  |
|  PLATO'S CRITIQUE                                                |
|  Gorgias: rhetoric is mere flattery, not real knowledge        |
|  Phaedrus: a philosophical rhetoric is possible but rare        |
|                                                                  |
|  ARISTOTLE'S SYNTHESIS (Rhetoric, c. 355-322 BCE)               |
|  Rhetoric is the counterpart (antistrophe) of dialectic         |
|  The enthymeme: the rhetorical syllogism                        |
|  Logos/Ethos/Pathos as the three means of persuasion           |
|  The topoi (topics/places): general argument-finding tools      |
|                                                                  |
|  ISOCRATES                                                       |
|  Rhetoric as education in civic virtue; the well-rounded orator |
+------------------------------------------------------------------+
```
